title: PR walkthroughs
lede: Every PR now explains itself with a page like this one. An agent writes the explanation, a script takes the code from git and refuses gaps it can detect, and you read the result before merging. The PR also corrects one false comment, found while writing the first walkthrough.

files.question: When is a walkthrough needed?
files.summary: The standing rule every agent session loads.
files.tested: Not enforced: it is an instruction.

files.question: What makes a good one?
files.summary: The procedure, the spec fields and the quality bar.
files.owns: How to write, check and link a walkthrough.

files.question: Is the page complete and current?
files.summary: Turns a spec plus git into HTML, or says why it will not.
files.owns: Reading git, resolving highlights, the refusals, the staleness check.
files.never: Judges whether an explanation is true.
files.tested: build.test.js, on real temporary git repos.

files.question: What does the reader see?
files.summary: The layout of your prototype, driven by data.
files.never: Reads git or loads anything from the network.
files.tested: No automated test. Clicked through by script in Chromium and Firefox.

files.question: Do the refusals work?
files.summary: Runs the real builder in throwaway repos.
files.never: Tests the look of the page.
files.tested: Each main check was broken on purpose to see a test fail.

files.question: Where do those tests run?
files.summary: One more glob in the unit project.

steps.title: The session starts
steps.explain: `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in every session, so the rule does not depend on anyone remembering this conversation.

steps.title: The agent commits, then writes the spec
steps.explain: Code is committed first because the page describes commits. The spec holds only words and pointers to code, never a copy of the code.

steps.title: The builder finds what changed
steps.explain: It compares HEAD with the merge base on `origin/main`. Numbered walkthroughs are left out, so committing the page does not make that page outdated.

steps.title: It reads the real code
steps.explain: Each file comes from `git show`, and the zero-context diff gives the line numbers to mark green.

steps.title: It resolves every highlight
steps.explain: A step quotes text instead of line numbers, which would drift. The text must match exactly one line, otherwise the highlight could land on the wrong code.

steps.title: It writes one HTML file
steps.explain: The data goes inside the template, so the page works offline. `<` is escaped, because code containing a closing script tag would otherwise end the script.

steps.title: The PR body links it
steps.explain: GitHub shows HTML as source, so the body carries a command that opens the page from the branch without a checkout.

steps.title: Code is not committed
steps.explain: The page would show HEAD while you look at newer code, so nothing is built.

steps.title: A changed file is not mentioned
steps.explain: Every changed file is either explained or listed with a reason. This stops a page from showing only the easy part of a diff.

steps.title: A shown file has no step
steps.explain: A tab full of code with no explanation is not a walkthrough.

steps.title: The explanation is simply wrong
steps.explain: **Nothing catches this.** The script proves that lines exist, not that the words are true. The guide asks for claims to be run, and your reading is the last check.

steps.title: A fix is pushed
steps.explain: The guide requires re-reading the steps and rebuilding, because correct lines under an old explanation still mislead.

steps.title: --check compares
steps.explain: It rebuilds in memory and compares with the committed file. A commit of only the page passes, and a code change fails.

run.to: is out of date: build it again

steps.title: CI does not run that check
steps.explain: CI runs the tests of the builder, but nothing fails a PR with a missing or outdated walkthrough. Today that depends on the agent following the rule.

steps.title: You choose a scenario and a step
steps.explain: The step opens the file of its first highlight. Dots on the other tabs show where else code runs.

steps.title: The code is painted
steps.explain: Highlighted lines are the ones in this step. Green numbers are the lines that this PR changed.

steps.title: You press an arrow key
steps.explain: The arrows move within the scenario and stop at either end.

steps.title: The old claim is tested
steps.explain: The comment said the API had to be under the base path to be inside the worker scope. In a scratch build with the API at `/api`, MSW still answered 200 in Chromium and Firefox. Scope limits the controlled pages, not their fetches.

steps.title: The code stays the same
steps.explain: The base path is still right: on GitHub Pages the rest of the origin belongs to other sites of the same account. Only the stated reason and the test name changed.

notes.title: Generated HTML is committed.
notes.detail: It opens with no build and stays as a record of each PR. The cost is one generated file per PR, which `.gitattributes` collapses in the diff.

notes.title: A script, not hand-written HTML.
notes.detail: Your prototype could afford a sketch. An explanation of real code cannot. The cost is a small tool to maintain and test.

notes.title: No CI enforcement.
notes.detail: That changes the merge gate, so it is left as a separate decision.

notes.title: Two concerns in one PR.
notes.detail: The comment fix is its own commit, so it can be split out or reverted alone.

notes.title: The spec repeats the false claim.
notes.detail: The API contract in issue #1 also says the base path keeps the API inside the worker scope. This PR does not edit the issue.
